$comment: Settings for an UNATTENDED run. The run owns its work end to end: branch, commit, push, open the pull request, poll CI, fix what CI finds, merge, continue to the next spec. It is stopped only from things that are unrecoverable, or that would let it escape review entirely.
$never: Do not add --bare to the launch command. Bare mode skips hooks, which removes the Stop gate that
is the entire basis for 'the agent cannot claim success', and it also bypasses stored credentials
so the run silently bills per token instead of using the subscription.
Do not use --permission-mode bypassPermissions or --dangerously-skip-permissions. Those permit
writes to protected paths, so the agent could delete the very guardrails meant to contain it.
Use dontAsk: it denies anything not explicitly allowed, never waits for input, and — critically —
denies the ask-a-question tool, so the only way out is finishing or writing BLOCKED.md.

$allowNotes.the-loop: A run does the whole job: creates its branch, commits, pushes, opens the pull request, polls CI, fixes what CI finds, merges when green, and moves on. Every one of those is allowed, because withholding any of them stops the loop rather than making it safer.
$allowNotes.why-merging-is-allowed: Merging is not the dangerous step. Merging something that has not passed the gates and the risk classifier is. Those checks run before the pull request opens and again in CI before it merges, so the merge is the conclusion of a verified process rather than an unguarded capability.
$allowNotes.reading-ci: `gh run view` and `gh run list` are allowed deliberately: a run that cannot read why CI failed cannot fix it, and fixing it is the point.

$denyNotes.unrecoverable: Force pushes, hard resets and history rewrites destroy work that no green test suite can bring back. Everything else a run does is a commit, and commits revert.
$denyNotes.escaping-review: Secrets, rulesets and workflow files are how a run could make itself unreviewable — by changing what CI checks, or by switching it off. Those stay closed. Reading workflow runs and logs stays open, because that is what fixing a failing check requires.
$denyNotes.dependencies: A new dependency is the highest-consequence thing a run can add, and the thing a prompt-injected agent would most want to add. A spec needing an unforeseen library ends BLOCKED — one morning decision.
$denyNotes.self-modification: Guardrails and gate definitions are off limits. A run that can edit its own gates has no gates.
$denyNotes.edit-and-write: Every protected path carries BOTH an Edit and a Write rule. Edit governs changing a file that exists; Write governs creating one. Guarding only Edit would leave a run free to drop a NEW hook into .claude/hooks/, which is as good as editing one.
$denyNotes.not-the-real-control: Treat these as a first line, not the line. Permission-rule semantics are the harness's, not ours, and a rule that silently does nothing looks exactly like a rule that works. The control that actually holds is the fingerprint run-spec.sh takes of every guarded path before the run and checks afterwards: if any of it moved, the run is TAMPERED and every other result from it is discarded, regardless of which permission rules fired.

$denyNotes: stacks/** was missing and is the one that mattered: each module's guard.json holds the production deny rules, and the risk policy, the classifier reading it and deliver-run.sh all live there too. A run could edit the thing that judges it. .claude/lib/** is here because the gate runner and the gate lock moved into it.
